strengths: The paper identifies and empirically substantiates an important and well-motivated problem: the 'vision shortcut' in VLA training. The three pilot experiments (Section 2) are a nice diagnostic contribution — e.g., the vision-only model retaining 44.6% success on RoboCasa vs 47.8% language-conditioned, and dropping to 12.4% on the ambiguous LIBERO Goal subset, clearly demonstrate that standard VLAs often ignore language.

The Bayesian formulation is elegant: decomposing the policy into a vision-only prior and a language-conditioned posterior, and maximizing the conditional PMI (LLR) between actions and instructions, gives a principled explanation of why standard likelihood training fails under deterministic v→ℓ coupling.

The implementation via Latent Action Queries and causal masking to enforce information separation between prior and posterior branches is a clever, practical design; at inference only the posterior branch is used, so there is no test-time overhead.
Strong empirical results: 66.5% avg on SimplerEnv (vs 55.2% same-framework baseline, +11.3%) and 50.4% on RoboCasa (vs 47.8%), outperforming strong recent systems like π0.5 and Isaac-GR00T-N1.6.
The ablation study (Table 3) usefully separates the architectural benefit of Action Queries (+2.3%) from the Bayesian objective (+6.0%), supporting the central hypothesis.

The qualitative demonstration (Figs. 4-5) that the LLR objective also preserves text-only conversational ability is an interesting secondary benefit, and the discussion of data collection strategies and world-model formulations is thoughtful.
Limitations are discussed honestly, including training overhead and the caveat that vision-language conversation can still degrade.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Table 1 reports BayesianVLA at 66.5% avg on SimplerEnv, but the ablation Table 3 reports the same method at 63.5%, with large per-task discrepancies (e.g., 89.6 vs 81.9 on 'Put Spoon'); the QwenGR00T baseline also differs (64.2 vs 54.2 on 'Put Eggplant'). No seeds, error bars, or explanation for these discrepancies are provided, despite evaluation randomness being acknowledged.

The experimental scope is overstated: Section 4 claims evaluation on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2', but no results are presented for LIBERO or RoboTwin2 (deferred to future work), and real-world experiments are absent. Notably, the method is never actually evaluated on LIBERO even though the LIBERO Goal ambiguity analysis motivates the entire approach.

The central causal claim — that gains come from improved language grounding rather than some other effect of the dual-branch/LLR training — is not directly verified. The most convincing evidence would be a post-hoc vision-only (language-masked) evaluation of BayesianVLA, analogous to the motivation experiments, but this is missing.

Theoretical treatment is loose. Eq. (3) shows I(ℓ;a|v) ≤ H(ℓ|v) ≈ 0 in goal-driven datasets, yet the proposed remedy is to 'maximize' this PMI, which is bounded near zero under the same data distribution; the tension between this bound and the LLR objective (and how the stop-gradient baseline prevents trivial gaming of Eq. 7) is not rigorously analyzed. The baseline p(ℓ|v) computation is described vaguely ('detaching gradients or using a separate pass').

Hyperparameter sensitivity for λ and β is not studied, and there is only one ablation benchmark. No evidence of robustness of the objective to different backbones or scales (8B experiments are future work).

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, results depend on the StarVLA framework with many unstated details, and the qualitative capability-preservation evidence is anecdotal (single examples) rather than benchmarked.

Some RoboCasa per-task results are inconsistent with the narrative (e.g., BayesianVLA underperforms the baseline on several tasks like 'PnP Novel From Cuttingboard To Pot' and 'From Plate To Bowl'), suggesting the aggregate gain is uneven; this is not discussed.

strengths: The motivating diagnosis is genuinely interesting: the three pilot experiments (vision-only success nearly matching language-conditioned success on RoboCasa, 12.4% vs ~95% on ambiguous LIBERO Goal, and near-0% OOD transfer from BridgeDataV2 to SimplerEnv) provide concrete empirical evidence for the 'vision shortcut' pathology, and this analysis is itself a useful community contribution.

The proposed method is practical in one important respect: the dual-branch structure is used only during training, so inference cost is unchanged relative to the baseline, and the latent action queries also reduce the action-head conditioning cost.

The core empirical claim is supported by a controlled comparison: the 11.3% improvement on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs 55.2%) is measured against a baseline built on the same StarVLA/QwenGR00T stack with matched training protocols, which isolates the contribution of the proposed objective better than cross-paper comparisons would.

The ablation (Table 3) appropriately separates the architectural benefit of action queries (+2.3%) from the Bayesian objective (+6.0% over the query-only variant), giving reasonable evidence that the objective, not just the architecture, drives the gain.

The limitations section is honest about the incomplete evaluation scope (no real-robot experiments, missing benchmarks) and about remaining degradation of vision-language (as opposed to text-only) capabilities.
weaknesses: The central theoretical argument is internally inconsistent. Section 2.4 derives that I(ℓ;a|v) ≤ H(ℓ|v) and that in goal-driven data H(ℓ|v) ≈ 0, so the conditional mutual information is 'forced to vanish.' But then the proposed fix is to maximize the very same conditional PMI/LLR on that same data — which by the paper's own bound carries no information to extract. The paper never explains how maximizing a quantity that is provably ≈ 0 on the training distribution can recover instruction-following; this gap undermines the framing that the method is a principled Bayesian intervention rather than a heuristic auxiliary loss.

The practical objective (Eq. 7) does not match the derived objective (Eq. 4). The derivation says to maximize log p(ℓ|a,v) − log p(ℓ|v) where a is the posterior action, but the implementation maximizes log p(ℓ|v, H_Q^prior) using the *prior* branch's action features, and the baseline p(ℓ|v) is described only vaguely ('detaching gradients or using a separate pass'). The connection between this implementation and PMI maximization is asserted, not shown, and potential degenerate solutions (e.g., Q tokens encoding instruction-predictive content independent of good actions) are not analyzed.

Numerical inconsistencies that are never explained: BayesianVLA achieves 66.5% on SimplerEnv in Table 1 but 63.5% in the ablation Table 3 (with per-task numbers differing by up to 7.7 points), yet no justification (different seeds, β/λ settings, etc.) is given. Section 4 also claims experiments on 'four simulation benchmarks' but only two (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa) are reported; RoboTwin2 and LIBERO are promised only as future work.

No statistical rigor: RoboCasa results use only 50 trials per task and SimplerEnv reports a single run; no seeds, variance, or confidence intervals are provided, despite per-task swings that are often within plausible noise (e.g., BayesianVLA loses to the VisionOnly baseline on several RoboCasa tasks).

Key implementation details needed for reproduction are missing: values of λ and β, how the LLR baseline is actually computed, learning-rate and branch-scheduling specifics, and no code release is mentioned despite building on an open framework.

Close prior work is not properly differentiated: Xu et al. (2025), 'Seeing to act, prompting to specify: A Bayesian factorization of vision language action policy' (arXiv:2512.11218), which is cited only in passing in Section 4.3, appears to address a substantially overlapping Bayesian factorization of VLA policies. The Related Work section does not discuss it, weakening the originality claims.

The claim of preserving general VLM capabilities rests on two cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figures 4 and 5); no quantitative language-understanding benchmark scores are reported, so the preservation claim is anecdotal.

Only one backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B within StarVLA) and one model scale are evaluated; comparisons against π0.5, Isaac-GR00T, etc., are cross-paper numbers under potentially different training data and tuning budgets, so 'state-of-the-art' claims are fragile. The limitations section concedes this but the abstract and contributions do not.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: the 'vision shortcut' / 'Information Collapse' pathology in VLA training, where language instructions become redundant given goal-driven dataset bias. The three pilot experiments (ID testing, ambiguous LIBERO Goal subset dropping to 12.4%, and near-0% OOD success) provide convincing empirical validation of the phenomenon.

The Bayesian decomposition framing (vision-only prior p(a|v) vs. language-conditioned posterior π(a|v,ℓ)) and the PMI/LLR objective is a clean and original lens on a practical failure mode, and the Appendix A derivation connecting the LLR to conditional PMI is correct.

The Latent Action Query mechanism is an elegant design: causal masking position controls information flow into the queries, enabling dual-branch training with a single shared VLM while incurring zero inference overhead.

Results are strong and multi-benchmark: +11.3% over the directly comparable QwenGR00T baseline on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs 55.2%, 480 trials/task) and a state-of-the-art 50.4% average on RoboCasa, beating Isaac-GR00T-N1.6 and OpenVLA-OFT.

The ablation (Table 3) properly separates the architectural contribution of action queries (+2.3%) from the Bayesian objective (+6.0%), supporting the central claim that the objective, not just the bottleneck architecture, drives gains.

The evaluation of general-capability preservation (Figs. 4-5) is a valuable addition often missing in VLA papers, and the honest discussion that vision-language (not just text-only) abilities may still degrade is commendable.
weaknesses: There is a conceptual gap between the theoretical objective and the practical loss. Eq. 4 motivates maximizing log π(a|v,ℓ)/p(a|v), but Eq. 7 instead maximizes log p(ℓ|v, H_Q^prior) − sg(log p(ℓ|v)). The paper itself is hand-wavy here ('we can compute a baseline p(ℓ|v) by detaching gradients or using a separate pass. However, a more direct and numerically stable approach is...'), so the actually-optimized objective is a variant whose equivalence to the stated PMI objective is not established. Additionally, Eq. 3 shows I(ℓ;a|v) ≤ H(ℓ|v) ≈ 0 under the very dataset bias being targeted, so the theoretical story of 'maximizing PMI' being possible on biased data is not fully resolved; gains may partly stem from regularization effects rather than the Bayesian narrative.

The experimental scope does not match the text. Section 4 promises results on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2', but only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are reported; no LIBERO or RoboTwin2 results appear, and real-robot experiments are absent ('currently underway').

The ablation study average (63.5% in Table 3) differs from the main SimplerEnv result (66.5% in Table 1) for the same BayesianVLA configuration without explanation, raising questions about run-to-run variance that is never quantified (no std/error bars or significance tests despite 480 trials).

No ablation of the two key hyperparameters λ and β, nor of the number of queries K, even though these directly control the objective trade-off central to the method. The complexity claim O(N²)→O(K²) for the DiT is asserted but not measured.

Gains on RoboCasa are more modest and uneven (50.4% vs 48.8% for OpenVLA-OFT), with BayesianVLA underperforming the baseline on several tasks (e.g., PnP Potato, Cuttingboard-to-Pot, Plate-to-Bowl), which deserves analysis.

The claimed marginal training overhead of the dual-branch setup is argued qualitatively but never quantified (no wall-clock or FLOP comparison), and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a method with nontrivial implementation choices (branch ordering, masking, stop-gradient placement).

strengths: The paper provides compelling empirical evidence for the 'vision shortcut' pathology: three carefully designed pilot experiments (ID testing, ambiguous LIBERO Goal scenes, OOD SimplerEnv) collectively demonstrate that standard VLA models can succeed without attending to language, and the quantitative conditional-entropy analysis (Table 7, NLL/PPL of instructions given vision) directly supports the information-collapse hypothesis rather than relying on anecdote alone.

The proposed LLR/PMI objective is instantiated in an architecturally elegant way: Latent Action Queries exploit causal masking to cleanly separate vision-only and vision-language contexts within a single shared backbone, enabling single-stage end-to-end training in contrast to the two-stage, frozen-prior design of BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which is clearly positioned as the closest prior work.

Evaluation is broad and mostly convincing: consistent gains on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs. 55.2% same-framework baseline), RoboCasa, LIBERO, and two real-robot pick-and-place settings with OOD held-out objects; the ablations are unusually thorough, including component ablations (Table 5), hyperparameter sweeps for both loss weights (Tables 11-12), number of queries (Table 13), and a well-conceived control experiment with an auxiliary p(ℓ|v) loss (Table 10) that distinguishes genuine action-relevant language grounding from mere language retention.

The paper includes an honest limitations section, a thoughtful data-collection discussion (Appendix C), and addresses the important practical concern of catastrophic forgetting of general VLM capabilities with qualitative evidence and a nuanced discussion of what is and is not preserved.

Reproducibility is reasonable: the method is described at implementation-level detail (loss weights, optimizer, distributed setup, training steps, evaluation protocols with 480/500 trials per setting), is built on the open StarVLA framework, and code/videos are promised for release.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing is looser than presented. Maximizing the pointwise log-ratio log π(a|v,ℓ) − log p(a|v) per sample is not the same as maximizing the conditional mutual information I(ℓ;a|v), and nothing in the objective directly ties high PMI to task success—a policy could satisfy the LLR objective with actions that are informative about ℓ yet incorrect. The practical loss (Eq. 7) further deviates from the derivation: the numerator is a language-modeling likelihood p(ℓ|v, H_prior_Q) computed in the prior branch, and the argument that the prior-branch queries 'encode action information a' via a detached prior is somewhat circular and under-justified. The derivation in Appendix A is algebraically fine but does not close this gap.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation errors undermine confidence: the abstract claims an 11.3% OOD improvement while the contribution list claims 8.8%; Section 4.5 refers to 'the full LangForce (63.5%)' where Table 5 reports 66.5%; Table 12's caption says 'Ablation study on β in Eq. 9' but its content is the λ sweep; and the Code link in the abstract is a placeholder ('available at this').

Several important experimental details are missing or thin: the claim that baseline numbers were 'obtained from their original papers or other peer-reviewed publications' means many SimplerEnv comparisons may differ in training data, backbone size, or evaluation protocol, and while the authors assert fairness, a same-protocol re-evaluation of at least one strong external baseline is not provided. The real-world evaluation is limited to two simple pick-and-place tasks with modest trial counts (30 per condition).

The mechanism by which the stop-gradient in Eq. 7 prevents degenerate solutions is asserted rather than analyzed; no ablation on the stop-gradient choice itself is reported, and the sensitivity of training to the LLR term (e.g., instability from maximizing a ratio) is not discussed beyond fixed β values.

The novelty is incremental relative to BayesVLA: the core Bayesian posterior/prior contrast exists in prior work, and the contribution is primarily a single-stage training scheme plus the query-bottleneck architecture. This is a useful and well-executed contribution, but the headline framing as identifying a new objective overstates the delta.

strengths: The motivating analysis (Section 2) is a genuine strength: three pilot experiments showing that a vision-only VLA nearly matches the language-conditioned model on ID benchmarks (44.6% vs 47.8% on RoboCasa; 9.8% vs 97.4% on ambiguous LIBERO Goal) provide concrete, policy-level evidence for the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon, which is useful for the community.

The evaluation is broad: SimplerEnv (480 trials), RoboCasa (50 trials/task), LIBERO, and two real-world Franka setups, with multiple ablations (loss weights, number of queries, auxiliary p(l|v) control), which exceeds the typical evaluation depth of many VLA post-training papers.

The method is architecturally elegant in one respect: exploiting causal masking to obtain both a vision-only prior and a language-conditioned posterior from a shared backbone at no inference-time cost, and the ablation on the auxiliary language-prediction control (Table 10) thoughtfully separates 'generic language retention' from 'action-relevant grounding'.
The limitations section is honest and the discussion of data-collection implications is thoughtful.
weaknesses: A core theoretical tension is never resolved: the paper argues that in goal-driven datasets H(l|v) ~ 0, and correctly notes I(l;a|v) <= H(l|v) (Eq. 3). But this means the very PMI objective the method maximizes is bounded near zero exactly in the training regime described. The paper does not explain why maximizing a near-vanishing quantity during training produces large behavioral gains, leaving the causal story behind the improvements unclear.

The connection between the derived objective (Eq. 4, an action-level LLR log p(l|a,v) - log p(l|v)) and the actually optimized loss (Eq. 7, a language-token LM-loss difference between two branches) is heuristic and under-justified. Eq. 7 uses H_prior_Q as a proxy for 'action a', but the relationship between the LM loss on instruction tokens and the true likelihood term is asserted rather than derived or empirically validated.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported numbers: the abstract claims an 11.3% improvement on OOD SimplerEnv while Contribution 3 claims 8.8%; Section 4.5 reports full LangForce at 63.5% while Table 5 lists 66.5%; Table 11's caption says 'Ablation study on beta' but it is the lambda ablation. Such sloppiness in the central results is concerning.

Baseline comparability is weak: many SimplerEnv numbers are copied from original papers with different training data, and the head-to-head evidence rests mainly on the StarVLA-internal QwenGR00T baseline. The gain of LangForce over 'VisionOnly' on RoboCasa (52.6% vs 44.7%) is modest, and on several task groups (e.g., 'From Cuttingboard' and 'From Tray') LangForce does not consistently beat simpler baselines.

Real-world evaluation is narrow: single-arm pick-and-place with 30 trials per condition, and the headline OOD result (9/30 vs 2/30 on an unseen red block) rests on very few trials; no confidence intervals are reported anywhere despite repeated claims of statistical significance.

Reproducibility is questionable: the 'Code and videos are available at this' link is a placeholder with no actual URL; no released checkpoints, and several key experimental details (e.g., exact LIBERO training protocol) are deferred or vague.

The 'preservation of general capabilities' claim (Section 4.4) is supported only by cherry-picked qualitative chat examples; no quantitative benchmark (e.g., MMLU, VQA suite) is used to measure forgetting, and Appendix B.4 concedes vision-language abilities may still degrade.

The paper's positioning against BayesVLA is fair, but the incremental novelty over existing shortcut/leakage analyses (e.g., Xing et al. 2025, which they cite) and Bayesian decomposition ideas is limited; the main new element is the query-position-based dual-branch implementation.

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically substantiates a well-motivated failure mode ('vision shortcut' / Information Collapse) in VLA training with three complementary pilot experiments (ID testing on RoboCasa, ambiguous LIBERO Goal, and OOD SimplerEnv), which grounds the method in evidence rather than assertion.

The Bayesian formulation is clean and the derivation in Appendix A is correct: maximizing conditional PMI between actions and instructions is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood ratio between the language-conditioned posterior and the vision-only prior, directly penalizing the collapse pi(a|v,l) ~ p(a|v).

The implementation is elegant and practical: Latent Action Queries exploit causal masking in a decoder-only VLM to instantiate prior and posterior branches with shared weights, incurring no inference overhead.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: SimplerEnv with 480 trials per task, RoboCasa with 50 trials per task over 24 tasks (full per-task table in Appendix), LIBERO, and two real-robot settings, with a large absolute improvement over the matched StarVLA baseline (66.5% vs 55.2% on SimplerEnv).

Ablations carefully isolate contributions: queries alone (+2.3), dual-branch without LLR (+6.1), full method (+11.3), plus sweeps over lambda, beta, and query count. The auxiliary p(l|v) control (Table 10) is a particularly good ablation showing that generic language retention does not explain the gains.

The analysis of preserved general language capabilities (Section 4.4, Appendix B.4) including the NLL/PPL analysis of H(l|v) on LIBERO Goal adds evidence that the mechanism works as theorized, and the limitations section is honest about training overhead and the restricted scope of real-world tasks.
weaknesses: Numerical inconsistencies undermine polish and raise trust concerns: the abstract reports 11.3% improvement while Contribution 3 claims 8.8%; Section 4.5 states 'full LangForce (63.5%)' when the method achieves 66.5%; Table 11/12 captions both say 'Ablation study on beta'.

No variance/seed reporting for the main simulation results; several margins are modest (LIBERO Goal +2.0%; RoboCasa 52.6% vs 48.8%), and per-task RoboCasa results show the vision-only baseline beating LangForce on several tasks, so single-run results leave uncertainty about robustness of the gains.
All results use a single backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B) within a single framework (StarVLA); generality of the dual-branch objective across architectures and scales is untested.

The closest prior work, BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also uses Bayesian decomposition for instruction following, is discussed but not compared empirically; the claimed advantage (single-stage end-to-end training) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The theoretical framing has a tension the paper only partially resolves: if I(l;a|v) <= H(l|v) ~ 0 on goal-driven data, per-sample PMI maximization cannot manufacture information that is absent from the data; the benefit presumably comes from preventing spurious v->l confidence, but this mechanistic account is more heuristic than proven, and the LM-loss proxy for the LLR (Eq. 7) is not validated directly against the true PMI.

Writing contains grammatical errors ('LangForce, enforces instruction following', 'across on three benchmarks'), and the claim of 'state-of-the-art' rests partly on numbers transplanted from other papers under possibly different training data mixes, despite the fair-comparison caveat.
